specStatements.text: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures. Melting point and boiling point data can be used to distinguish pure substances from mixtures.
In everyday language, a pure substance can mean a substance that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk.
Students should be able to use melting point and boiling point data to distinguish pure from impure substances.

A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product. Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose. Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties. Formulations include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods.
Students should be able to identify formulations given appropriate information.
Students do not need to know the names of components in proprietary products.

Chromatography can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances. Chromatography involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase. Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases.
The ratio of the distance moved by a compound (centre of spot from origin) to the distance moved by the solvent can be expressed as its Rf value:
R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent)

Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, which can be used to help identify the compounds. The compounds in a mixture may separate into different spots depending on the solvent but a pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents.
explain how paper chromatography separates mixtures
suggest how chromatographic methods can be used for distinguishing pure substances from impure substances
interpret chromatograms and determine Rf values from chromatograms
provide answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
Required practical 6: investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances. Students should calculate Rf values.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of components in proprietary products.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Formulations are taught only through the categories the specification itself lists (fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods) and through the idea that each component is present in a measured quantity for a particular purpose. Where a product appears in a stem, its components are described by the job they do (pigment, binder, solvent) or given as unnamed percentages, never as the recipe of a named brand. No item in this topic asks a student to recall what is inside any commercial paint, detergent, medicine, fertiliser or food, and no concept, misconception or option lists such ingredients. Judgement is always about whether the information given describes a mixture made to measured quantities for a purpose.

concepts.definition: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. Purity is a statement about what is in the sample, not about how clean, clear or natural it looks.

Two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined. The substances keep their own properties, which is why a mixture melts and boils over a range of temperatures rather than at one temperature.

In everyday language a pure substance is one that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk. Such a substance is almost always a mixture in the chemical sense.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes from solid to liquid. A pure substance melts sharply at that one temperature rather than over a range.
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes from liquid to gas. A pure liquid boils steadily at that one temperature while it all turns to gas.

concepts.term: Using melting and boiling data to test purity
concepts.definition: Compare the measured value with the data book value for the pure substance, and look at whether the change happens at one temperature or over a range. An impurity lowers a melting point and raises a boiling point, and in both cases spreads the change over a range.
A mixture that has been designed as a useful product. Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose.

Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties. Change the proportions and the product no longer does its job properly.
Formulations include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. Each is a mixture, so a formulation is never a pure substance.
A technique that can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances. It involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
The phase that does not move. In paper chromatography the paper is the stationary phase, and a substance attracted strongly to it is held back near the origin.
The phase that moves. In paper chromatography the solvent is the mobile phase, and it carries dissolved substances up the paper as it rises.

Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases. A substance more attracted to the solvent than to the paper spends more time moving and travels further; a substance held more strongly by the paper travels less far.

The ratio of the distance moved by a compound (centre of spot from origin) to the distance moved by the solvent: R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent). It is a ratio of two distances, so it has no units and is always less than 1.

Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, which can be used to help identify the compounds. The compounds in a mixture may separate into different spots depending on the solvent, but a pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents.
The pencil line on which the samples are spotted. The distance moved by a compound is measured from this line to the centre of its spot.
The furthest point the solvent reaches up the paper, marked in pencil as soon as the paper is taken out. The distance moved by the solvent is measured from the origin to this line.

concepts.term: Significant figures in an Rf value
concepts.definition: An answer is given to an appropriate number of significant figures, which means no more than the measurements it came from. Distances read to two significant figures give an Rf value quoted to two significant figures.

Investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances, calculating Rf values. The start line is drawn in pencil and the solvent in the container starts below that line.

misconceptions.question: A carton is labelled pure orange juice. Is the juice pure in the chemical sense?
misconceptions.correct: No. Nothing has been added to it, which is the everyday meaning of pure, but chemically it is a mixture of water, sugars, acids and many other compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: If a label says pure then the contents must be a single chemical substance, because pure means the same thing in science as it does on packaging.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification's own point is that the two meanings differ. Advertising uses pure to mean unadulterated and natural, and students meet that use thousands of times before they meet the chemical definition once.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what is in the sample, not what has been done to it. Chemically pure means one element or one compound and nothing else, so orange juice is a mixture whatever the carton claims.

misconceptions.question: Clean air contains nitrogen, oxygen and argon, all of which are pure elements. Is clean air pure?
misconceptions.correct: No. Air contains several different substances mixed together, so it is a mixture however pure each separate gas is.
misconceptions.misconception: A sample built out of pure substances must itself be pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat purity as a property that each component carries and that survives mixing, rather than as a count of how many substances are present.
misconceptions.correction: Count the substances. One element or one compound is pure; two or more not chemically combined is a mixture, no matter how pure each one was on its own.

misconceptions.question: A blue copper sulfate solution is completely clear with nothing floating in it. Is it pure?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a mixture of copper sulfate and water; being clear and uniform tells you nothing about how many substances are present.
misconceptions.misconception: If a sample looks clear and uniform and has no visible bits, it must be a pure substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language uses clear and clean as synonyms for pure, and dissolved substances are invisible, so the eye gives no evidence either way.
misconceptions.correction: Appearance is not evidence of purity. Use melting point or boiling point data, or chromatography, to find out how many substances are really there.

misconceptions.question: A solid melts gradually between 118 °C and 124 °C. Does that show it is pure?
misconceptions.correct: No. A pure substance melts at one specific temperature; melting over a range shows the sample is impure.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting over a range is normal for any solid, so a range is not evidence of impurity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In the lab even pure samples take time to melt, so students read the time taken as a temperature range and stop treating a sharp melting point as the test.
misconceptions.correction: Watch the thermometer, not the clock. Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures, so a spread of several degrees means more than one substance is present.

misconceptions.question: Pure aspirin melts at 135 °C. A sample melts from 122 °C to 128 °C. What has the impurity done?
misconceptions.correct: It has lowered the melting point and spread it over a range.
misconceptions.misconception: Impurities always raise the melting point, because there is now more material that has to melt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the salt-and-water boiling result, where the boiling point rises, straight across to melting, and adding something feels as though it should make melting harder.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the two effects separately: an impurity lowers a melting point and raises a boiling point, and in both cases spreads the change over a range instead of one temperature.

misconceptions.question: Sea water boils above 100 °C and the temperature keeps rising as it boils. What does that show?
misconceptions.correct: It is a mixture. A pure liquid boils steadily at one specific temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Sea water is just water with a new, higher fixed boiling point, so the data still describe a pure substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The single quoted value for salt water in textbooks hides the range, and students remember only that salt raises the boiling point.
misconceptions.correction: Look for a steady temperature during boiling. A rising temperature while a liquid boils is the signature of a mixture, whatever the starting value was.

misconceptions.question: A sample melts from 122 °C to 128 °C and the data book value for the pure compound is 135 °C. A student says the average, 125 °C, is close enough to call it pure. Is it?
misconceptions.correct: No. The value is 10 °C low and the melting happens over a range, and both point to an impure sample.
misconceptions.misconception: If the measured temperature is anywhere near the data book value, the sample counts as pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are used to accepting measurements within experimental error, and averaging a range into a single number throws away the very evidence the range carries.
misconceptions.correction: Judge two things: how far the value sits from the data book value, and whether the change happened at one temperature or over a range. A range is decisive on its own.

misconceptions.question: Carbon dioxide contains two different elements. Does that make it a mixture?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its atoms are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, so it is a compound, and a compound is a pure substance.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything containing more than one element must be a mixture, so only elements can be pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word mixture is heard as containing different things, and the chemical bonding that separates a compound from a mixture is invisible in a formula such as CO2.
misconceptions.correction: A pure substance is a single element or a single compound. In a compound the elements are chemically bonded in fixed proportions and cannot be separated by filtering or evaporating.

misconceptions.question: Is sea water a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a mixture, but nobody designed it or measured out its components for a purpose.
misconceptions.misconception: Every mixture is a formulation, because a formulation is defined as a mixture.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students latch onto the first half of the definition and drop the qualifier that a formulation is designed as a useful product with its components in measured quantities.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the whole definition. Ask whether someone chose the components, measured them out and made the product for a purpose. Sea water fails that test; a paint or a fertiliser passes it.

misconceptions.question: Can a solid or a gas be a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The specification lists alloys and foods among formulations, and a fuel may be a mixture of gases.
misconceptions.misconception: Formulations have to be liquids, such as paints, medicines and cleaning agents.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The examples students meet first are usually liquids in bottles with ingredient lists, so the state of matter gets bundled into the definition.
misconceptions.correction: State of matter is irrelevant. What matters is that the components were mixed in measured quantities to make a useful product.

misconceptions.question: Is an alloy a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. An alloy is a mixture of metals blended in measured proportions to give properties such as extra hardness, and the specification lists alloys as formulations.
misconceptions.misconception: Alloys cannot be formulations because metals are elements, so an alloy is a pure metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alloys look like a single shiny metal with no visible components, and students met them as materials rather than as mixtures.
misconceptions.correction: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Because the amounts are chosen and measured to give the properties wanted, it fits the definition of a formulation exactly.

misconceptions.question: Distilled water is sold as a useful product for steam irons. Is it a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a single compound, and a formulation must be a mixture of components that each do a job.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything manufactured and sold as a useful product counts as a formulation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the words useful product from the definition and treat being on sale as the whole test.
misconceptions.correction: Check for a mixture first. If the product is one element or one compound it cannot be a formulation, however carefully it was made or however useful it is.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter how much of each component goes into a formulation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The components are mixed in carefully measured quantities so that the product has the properties it needs.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the list of ingredients matters; the proportions can be varied freely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recipes at home tolerate rough quantities, and ingredient lists on packaging give names without amounts, so the measuring is invisible.
misconceptions.correction: The proportions are part of the design. Change them and the paint runs, the fuel misfires or the medicine gives the wrong dose, so the product no longer has the required properties.

misconceptions.question: In paper chromatography, which is the stationary phase and which is the mobile phase?
misconceptions.correct: The paper is the stationary phase and the solvent is the mobile phase.
misconceptions.misconception: The paper is the mobile phase, because the solvent sits still in the beaker while the paper does the work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students watch the paper being the active piece of apparatus and see a beaker of solvent standing still, so the labels get attached to the wrong objects.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what physically moves during the run. The solvent travels up the paper, so the solvent is mobile and the paper, which never moves, is stationary.

misconceptions.question: Is the ink being separated the mobile phase?
misconceptions.correct: No. The mobile phase is the solvent. The ink is the mixture being separated, and it is distributed between the two phases.
misconceptions.misconception: The dyes are the mobile phase because they are the things moving up the paper, and anything that dissolves travels all the way to the solvent front.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The spots are what students watch, so movement gets identified with them, and it is easy to assume that dissolving is all that matters.
misconceptions.correction: The two phases are the paper and the solvent. The dyes are the sample, and each one is shared between the phases to a different extent, which is why they end up at different heights.

misconceptions.question: Do the substances separate because the paper acts as a sieve?
misconceptions.correct: No. Separation depends on the distribution of each substance between the paper and the solvent.
misconceptions.misconception: The paper has tiny holes, so small particles pass through it quickly and large ones are trapped near the start line.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filtration is the separation method students meet first, and paper is used there as a sieve, so the mechanism is carried across to chromatography.
misconceptions.correction: Nothing passes through the paper in chromatography; the solvent moves along it. How far a substance goes depends on how strongly it is attracted to the paper compared with the solvent.

misconceptions.question: Does the heaviest substance in a mixture travel furthest up the paper?
misconceptions.correct: No. Distance travelled depends on the distribution between the phases, not on how heavy the substance is.
misconceptions.misconception: Heavy substances are dragged back down by gravity, so the lightest dye always ends up highest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gravity is the everyday explanation for anything that fails to rise, and students have no other model to hand for why a spot stopped where it did.
misconceptions.correction: Explain the height by attraction: a substance held strongly by the paper moves a short way, and one that stays dissolved in the moving solvent moves far.

misconceptions.question: A spot moved 3.6 cm and the solvent moved 9.0 cm. Is the Rf value 9.0 / 3.6?
misconceptions.correct: No. R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent), so it is 3.6 / 9.0 = 0.40.
misconceptions.misconception: Rf is the solvent distance divided by the substance distance, so the bigger number goes on top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recall that Rf compares two distances but not which way round, and dividing the larger by the smaller feels like the natural thing to do.
misconceptions.correction: The solvent always travels furthest, so it belongs on the bottom of the fraction. Put the substance distance on top and every Rf value comes out less than 1.

misconceptions.question: Should an Rf value be written with units, for example 0.40 cm?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rf is a ratio of two distances, so the units cancel and it has no units.
misconceptions.misconception: Rf is a distance up the paper, so it must be quoted in centimetres.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both measurements that go into it are in centimetres, and students are rightly drilled to attach units to every answer.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing cm by cm leaves a bare number. Write the Rf value as a number alone, with no unit after it.

misconceptions.question: Can an Rf value be greater than 1?
misconceptions.correct: No. The solvent always moves further than any spot, so the top of the fraction is smaller than the bottom.
misconceptions.misconception: An Rf value of 2.5 is a perfectly reasonable answer; Rf values can be any size.
misconceptions.whyItArises: If the fraction has been inverted, or the distances combined some other way, the answer comes out above 1 and there is no unit to look wrong, so nothing signals the error.
misconceptions.correction: Use Rf below 1 as a check on your own arithmetic. An answer above 1 means the two distances have been combined the wrong way round.

misconceptions.question: Does a compound have one fixed Rf value?
misconceptions.correct: No. Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, so an Rf value only means something alongside the solvent used.
misconceptions.misconception: Rf is a constant for a substance, like its melting point, so it can be looked up whatever the solvent.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rf values are given in tables that look like data book constants, and the solvent is often left out of the question.
misconceptions.correction: Always record the solvent with the Rf value. Comparing a sample with a reference is only valid when both were run in the same solvent on the same paper.

misconceptions.question: A sample gives one spot in one solvent. Does that prove it is a pure compound?
misconceptions.correct: Not on its own. A pure compound produces a single spot in all solvents, so the run should be repeated in other solvents.
misconceptions.misconception: One spot in one solvent is proof of purity, so there is no need to run the sample again.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One spot looks like a complete result, and students do not expect two substances to happen to travel the same distance.
misconceptions.correction: Two compounds can have very similar Rf values in one solvent and separate clearly in another. Only a single spot in every solvent tried supports purity.

misconceptions.question: Two dyes give the same Rf value in one solvent. Are they the same compound?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. They should be run again in a different solvent, where different compounds are likely to separate.
misconceptions.misconception: Matching Rf values in a single solvent identify a substance for certain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rf is presented as a way of identifying compounds, so a match reads as an identification rather than as evidence that still has to be confirmed.
misconceptions.correction: Treat one matching Rf value as consistent with, not proof of, being the same compound. Confirm it by running both again in a different solvent.

misconceptions.question: Which part of a spot do you measure to?
misconceptions.correct: The centre of the spot, measured from the pencil line where the sample was placed.
misconceptions.misconception: Measure to the top edge of the spot, since that is as far as the substance reached.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Spots spread as they travel, and the leading edge is easier to see than the middle, so it becomes the obvious thing to measure.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines the distance as the centre of the spot from the origin. Measuring to an edge inflates the Rf value and gives a different answer for the same spot.

misconceptions.question: Where do the distances start from?
misconceptions.correct: Both are measured from the pencil start line, the origin, not from the bottom edge of the paper.
misconceptions.misconception: The distances are measured from the bottom of the paper, where the solvent actually started.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The solvent really does begin at the bottom of the sheet, so measuring from there feels more honest than measuring from a drawn line.
misconceptions.correction: Use the same starting line for both measurements. Measuring from the paper's edge adds an extra centimetre or two to each distance and changes the Rf value.

misconceptions.question: Why is the start line drawn in pencil rather than pen?
misconceptions.correct: Pencil is insoluble in the solvent, so it stays put instead of running up the paper and confusing the chromatogram.
misconceptions.misconception: Pencil is used only because it is easier to see, or because ink would react chemically with the solvent.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn the rule as a piece of exam ritual without the reason, then invent a plausible one such as visibility or a reaction.
misconceptions.correction: The reason is solubility, not visibility or reactivity. Ink is itself a mixture of dyes that would dissolve and separate, adding spots of its own to the paper.

misconceptions.question: A calculator shows 0.457627 for an Rf value worked out from 2.7 cm and 5.9 cm. What should be written down?
misconceptions.correct: 0.46, because the measurements were given to two significant figures.
misconceptions.misconception: Copying the whole calculator display makes the answer more accurate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: More digits look more precise, and students are reluctant to throw away figures the calculator has supplied.
misconceptions.correction: An answer cannot be more precise than the measurements behind it. Two-significant-figure distances give a two-significant-figure Rf value.

misconceptions.question: Why must the solvent in the container start below the pencil line?
misconceptions.correct: If the solvent is above the line the samples dissolve straight into it and wash off the paper instead of travelling up it.
misconceptions.misconception: The solvent level does not matter, or a deeper solvent simply makes the run faster and neater.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is easy to break when the beaker is filled first, and the failure looks like a poor result rather than a broken method.
misconceptions.correction: Set the depth so that the solvent starts below the spots. It then rises through them and carries them up the paper, which is the whole point of the run.

misconceptions.question: Is the bottom of the Rf fraction the length of the paper?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the distance moved by the solvent, measured from the origin to the solvent front.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide by the height of the paper, because that is how far the spot could have gone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The paper is the obvious fixed length in front of the student, and the solvent front is only a faint pencil mark that is easy to ignore.
misconceptions.correction: Mark the solvent front in pencil as soon as the paper comes out, and measure to that line. The solvent almost never reaches the top of the paper.

mcqs.stem: In the chemical sense of the word, which of these samples is pure?

options.text: Distilled water, which contains only the compound H2O
options.rationale: A pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance, and distilled water is only H2O.

options.text: Sea water, because it is clear and colourless
options.rationale: Being clear says nothing about how many substances are present; sea water is water plus several dissolved salts.

options.text: Spring water bottled with nothing added at all
options.rationale: This is the everyday meaning of pure, unadulterated and natural, but spring water contains dissolved minerals.

options.text: Clean air, since each of the gases in it is pure
options.rationale: Purity does not survive mixing; air holds nitrogen, oxygen and argon together, so it is a mixture.

mcqs.stem: A student says carbon dioxide must be a mixture because it contains two different elements. Why is the student wrong?

options.text: It is a colourless gas, and colourless gases are pure
options.rationale: Appearance is not evidence of purity; plenty of colourless gases, such as air, are mixtures.

options.text: Carbon and oxygen are pure, so this gas is pure
options.rationale: This treats purity as something the components carry into the product, which would make air pure too.

options.text: Its atoms are chemically bonded in fixed proportions
options.rationale: A pure substance is a single element or compound, and in a compound the elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions.

options.text: Its elements are unbonded and too small to split
options.rationale: The elements in carbon dioxide are chemically bonded, and a mixture is not defined by how hard it is to separate.

mcqs.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that a solid sample is pure?

options.text: It melts gradually over a range of several degrees
options.rationale: A melting range is the signature of a mixture, not of a pure substance.

options.text: It melts sharply at one specific temperature
options.rationale: Pure elements and compounds melt at specific temperatures, so a sharp melting point is the evidence wanted.

options.text: It is a fine white powder with no visible specks
options.rationale: A uniform appearance is not evidence of purity; many mixtures look completely uniform.

options.text: It melts at a temperature well over 100 °C
options.rationale: A high melting point is a property of the substance, not a test of how many substances are present.

mcqs.stem: A sample of sea water starts to boil at 102 °C and the temperature keeps rising while it boils. What does this show?

options.text: Salt gives the water a new fixed boiling point
options.rationale: A pure liquid boils steadily at one temperature, so a rising temperature rules this out.

options.text: The water in it is a different compound
options.rationale: The water is the same compound; the changed behaviour comes from the dissolved salts.

options.text: It is pure, since nothing was added to it
options.rationale: That is the everyday meaning of pure; chemically the sample contains water and several salts.

options.text: It is a mixture, not a pure substance
options.rationale: Boiling over a range rather than at one specific temperature is how boiling point data reveal a mixture.

mcqs.stem: A carton of milk is labelled pure milk. What does the word pure mean on that label?

options.text: It holds only one compound, so it is chemically pure
options.rationale: Milk is a mixture of water, fats, sugars and proteins; the label is not making a chemical claim.

options.text: Nothing has been added to it, so it is in its natural state
options.rationale: In everyday language a pure substance is one that is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk.

options.text: It has been filtered until only water and fat are left
options.rationale: The label says nothing has been put in or taken out; it does not describe any purification step.

options.text: Every part of it looks the same, so it is one substance
options.rationale: A uniform appearance is not what the label claims, and it would not prove purity if it were.

mcqs.stem: Pure aspirin melts at 135 °C. A student's prepared sample melts between 122 °C and 128 °C. What do the data show?

options.text: It is pure aspirin, since the average is close to the book value
options.rationale: Averaging the range hides the evidence; the value is 10 °C low and the melting is spread out.

options.text: It is pure, because pure solids melt over a range of degrees
options.rationale: Pure elements and compounds melt at specific temperatures, so a range indicates the opposite.

options.text: It is impure, because an impurity raises the melting point
options.rationale: The conclusion is right but the reasoning is wrong: impurities lower melting points and raise boiling points.

options.text: It is impure: the impurity lowered and spread the melting point
options.rationale: An impurity lowers a melting point and spreads it over a range, which is what these data show.

mcqs.stem: Four liquids were heated to boiling. Which behaviour identifies a pure liquid?

options.text: It boils steadily at 78 °C until it has all gone
options.rationale: A pure compound boils at a specific temperature, which stays constant throughout boiling.

options.text: It boils at 100 °C and leaves a white solid behind
options.rationale: The solid left behind was dissolved in the liquid all along, so the liquid was a mixture.

options.text: It boils away over a range from 78 °C to 91 °C
options.rationale: Boiling over a range shows that more than one substance is present.

options.text: It starts to boil at 95 °C and the temperature rises
options.rationale: A rising temperature during boiling is the signature of a mixture, whatever the starting value.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the definition of a formulation?

options.text: Any mixture containing two or more substances
options.rationale: This drops the design and the measured quantities, so it would make sea water and muddy water formulations.

options.text: A compound made by mixing elements together
options.rationale: A compound is a pure substance made by reaction, not by mixing components in measured amounts.

options.text: A mixture designed as a useful product
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: a formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product.

options.text: A pure substance made to an exact recipe
options.rationale: A formulation is always a mixture; a pure substance cannot be one however carefully it is made.

mcqs.stem: Why are the components of a formulation mixed in carefully measured quantities?

options.text: So the mixture becomes one pure compound as it is stirred
options.rationale: Mixing does not make a compound, and a formulation stays a mixture of its components.

options.text: So the components all react and leave no waste behind
options.rationale: The components are not there to react with each other; each has its own job in the product.

options.text: So the product has exactly the properties it was designed to have
options.rationale: The quantities are part of the design, and the proportions are what give the product its required properties.

options.text: They need not be measured; only the ingredients matter
options.rationale: Change the proportions and the paint runs or the medicine gives the wrong dose, so the amounts do matter.

mcqs.stem: A student is given information about four substances. Which one is a formulation?

options.text: A paint with pigment, binder and solvent in fixed amounts
options.rationale: Components with particular purposes, mixed in measured quantities to make a useful product, define a formulation.

options.text: Sea water, a mixture of water and many different dissolved salts
options.rationale: It is a mixture, but nobody designed it or measured out its components for a purpose.

options.text: Distilled water sold in bottles for topping up an iron
options.rationale: It is a useful product, but it is a single compound rather than a mixture.

options.text: Nitrogen taken from air and used to fill food packets
options.rationale: Nitrogen is a single element with a use; a formulation has to be a mixture of components.

mcqs.stem: A jeweller melts 75% gold with measured amounts of copper and silver to make a harder gold alloy. Is the alloy a formulation?

options.text: No, because a formulation has to be a liquid such as a paint
options.rationale: State of matter is irrelevant; the specification lists alloys and foods as formulations.

options.text: No, because metals are elements, so alloys are pure
options.rationale: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, not a pure substance.

options.text: Yes, because the metals react to form a new hard compound
options.rationale: The conclusion is right but the reason is wrong: the metals are mixed, not chemically combined.

options.text: Yes: measured amounts are mixed to give a useful product
options.rationale: Components in carefully measured quantities give the required property, hardness, so this is a formulation.

mcqs.stem: In paper chromatography, which phase is stationary and which is mobile?

options.text: Solvent stationary, the dyes are mobile
options.rationale: Both labels are wrong: the dyes are the sample being separated, and the solvent is what moves.

options.text: Paper stationary, solvent mobile
options.rationale: The paper never moves and the solvent rises through it, so the paper is stationary and the solvent mobile.

options.text: Paper stationary, the ink is mobile
options.rationale: The ink is the mixture being separated; the mobile phase is the solvent that carries it.

options.text: Solvent stationary, the paper mobile
options.rationale: The solvent is the phase that moves; the paper stays where it is throughout the run.

mcqs.stem: Why do the substances in a mixture end up at different heights on a chromatogram?

options.text: Heavier substances are pulled back down the paper by gravity
options.rationale: Height does not depend on mass, and gravity is not what stops a spot travelling.

options.text: The smallest particles fit through the gaps in the paper first
options.rationale: Nothing passes through the paper; this is filtration reasoning applied to the wrong technique.

options.text: Each substance dissolves in a different part of the solvent
options.rationale: The solvent is a single liquid with no separate parts for substances to choose between.

options.text: They are distributed differently between the paper and the solvent
options.rationale: Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the stationary and mobile phases.

mcqs.stem: What does the Rf value of a compound compare?

options.text: The distance the spot moved up the paper, in centimetres
options.rationale: Rf is a ratio of two distances, not a single distance, so it is a number with no units.

options.text: How far the compound moved against how far the solvent moved
options.rationale: Rf is the ratio of the distance moved by the compound to the distance moved by the solvent.

options.text: How far the spot moved against the length of the paper
options.rationale: The bottom of the fraction is the distance moved by the solvent, not the length of the paper.

options.text: How far the solvent moved against how far the compound spot went
options.rationale: This is the fraction upside down, and it gives answers greater than 1.

mcqs.stem: Which equation gives the Rf value of a substance?

options.text: Rf = distance moved by substance x distance moved up by solvent
options.rationale: Multiplying two distances gives an area, and the answer would be far greater than 1.

options.text: Rf = distance moved by substance / total length of paper
options.rationale: The denominator is the distance moved by the solvent, measured to the solvent front.

options.text: Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
options.rationale: This is the equation exactly as the specification gives it.

options.text: Rf = distance moved by the solvent / distance moved by substance
options.rationale: Inverting the fraction always gives a value above 1, which no Rf value can be.

mcqs.stem: A sample is run in three different solvents and gives one spot each time. What does this show?

options.text: The sample is a pure compound
options.rationale: A pure compound produces a single spot in all solvents, which is what has been found here.

options.text: The sample must be a single element
options.rationale: One spot shows one compound, but chromatography cannot tell an element from a compound.

options.text: The spots have simply overlapped
options.rationale: Two substances might coincide in one solvent, but not in three different solvents.

options.text: All three solvents are the same
options.rationale: Different solvents give different Rf values, so identical spots do not mean identical solvents.

mcqs.stem: Two dyes give the same Rf value in one solvent. What should the student do next?

options.text: Run them again in a different solvent and compare
options.rationale: Different compounds usually have different Rf values in a different solvent, so this tests the match.

options.text: Repeat the run in the same solvent for longer
options.rationale: A longer run in the same solvent moves both spots together and gives no new information.

options.text: Conclude that the dyes are the same compound
options.rationale: One matching Rf value is consistent with a match but does not prove it.

options.text: Decide that both of the dyes must be pure
options.rationale: The question is whether the dyes are the same, and one solvent cannot establish purity either.

mcqs.stem: A dye is held strongly by the paper and dissolves only slightly in the solvent. On the chromatogram this dye will

options.text: travel with the solvent front, as dissolved dyes do
options.rationale: Dissolving is not enough; a dye is shared between the phases, and this one is held by the paper.

options.text: stay on the line, unable to enter the paper
options.rationale: Nothing passes through the paper, and a slightly soluble dye still creeps up it a little.

options.text: move furthest of all, being the lightest one
options.rationale: Distance travelled depends on the distribution between the phases, not on how heavy the dye is.

options.text: move only a short way up, giving a low Rf value
options.rationale: Strong attraction to the stationary phase keeps the dye near the origin, so its Rf value is small.

mcqs.stem: A chromatogram is run on a food colouring. Which result shows that the colouring is impure?

options.text: The colouring gives one spot of high Rf value
options.rationale: A single spot points towards a pure compound, and the size of the Rf value says nothing about purity.

options.text: The colouring separates into more than one spot
options.rationale: The compounds in a mixture separate into different spots, so several spots show the sample is impure.

options.text: Its spot is bigger than the spot of the reference dye
options.rationale: Spot size depends on how much sample was loaded, not on how many substances it contains.

options.text: Its Rf value differs from the reference dye's value
options.rationale: A different Rf value means a different compound, which can still be a pure one.

mcqs.stem: When finding an Rf value from a chromatogram, how is the distance moved by the substance measured?

options.text: From the bottom edge of the paper to the spot
options.rationale: Both distances are measured from the pencil origin, not from the edge of the paper.

options.text: From the pencil line to the top of the spot
options.rationale: Measuring to the leading edge instead of the centre inflates the Rf value.

options.text: From the pencil line to the spot's centre
options.rationale: The specification defines the distance as the centre of the spot measured from the origin.

options.text: From the solvent front down to the spot centre
options.rationale: This measures what is left of the run, not how far the substance travelled from the origin.

mcqs.stem: On a chromatogram a spot has moved 3.6 cm from the pencil line and the solvent has moved 9.0 cm. What is the Rf value of the spot?

options.text: 5.4 cm, the difference of the two
options.rationale: Rf is a ratio, not a difference, and it never carries a unit.

options.text: 2.5, worked out as 9.0 cm / 3.6 cm
options.rationale: The fraction is upside down; the solvent distance belongs on the bottom.

options.text: 0.40, worked out as 3.6 cm / 9.0 cm
options.rationale: R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent) = 3.6 / 9.0 = 0.40.

options.text: 0.40 cm, since Rf is a distance
options.rationale: The arithmetic is right, but dividing cm by cm leaves a number with no units.

mcqs.stem: A spot moved 2.7 cm and the solvent moved 5.9 cm. The calculator shows 0.457627 for the Rf value. How should the answer be given?

options.text: 0.46, matching the two significant figures measured
options.rationale: An answer is quoted to no more significant figures than the measurements it came from.

options.text: 0.4576, since the extra digits make it more accurate
options.rationale: Extra digits from the calculator cannot add precision the ruler never supplied.

options.text: 0.457627, exactly as the calculator displays it
options.rationale: Six figures claim a precision far beyond distances read to the nearest millimetre.

options.text: 0.5, rounded to just one significant figure
options.rationale: One significant figure throws away a figure that the measurements do support.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 6, why is the start line on the chromatography paper drawn in pencil?

options.text: Ink would react with the solvent to make a new dye
options.rationale: No reaction takes place; the problem with ink is that it dissolves and travels.

options.text: Pencil is easier to see against the coloured dyes
options.rationale: Visibility is not the reason, and pencil is in fact fainter than ink.

options.text: Pencil holds the spots in place on the line
options.rationale: The spots are meant to move; the line only marks the origin and holds nothing.

options.text: Pencil does not dissolve and move up the paper
options.rationale: Pencil is insoluble in the solvent, so the line stays put instead of separating into spots of its own.

mcqs.stem: Why must the solvent in the beaker start below the pencil line on the paper?

options.text: Otherwise the paper would sink to the beaker's base
options.rationale: The paper is supported at the top; its position does not depend on the depth of solvent.

options.text: Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent
options.rationale: Solvent above the line washes the samples off the paper instead of carrying them up it.

options.text: Otherwise the solvent front would end up uneven
options.rationale: An uneven front comes from a tilted paper or an uncovered beaker, not from the depth.

options.text: Otherwise the solvent would rise too fast up the paper
options.rationale: A deeper solvent does not speed the run up; the problem is that the spots are washed away.
